body_html:
My March stock pick sits at the core of a thesis I have been building since late last year: the energy sector is undervalued, and the best way to profit from this mispricing is not to bet on the commodity itself, but to own the picks and shovels.

This should be a familiar theme if you have been following my writing for a while. Rather than investing in Nvidia [] directly, I invested in the infrastructure that makes Nvidia possible: the advanced node manufacturer (), the data center builders (, ), the power suppliers keeping those centers running (), the memory providers (), and the rack manufacturer on which those Nvidia chips sit (). The same logic applies here. I am not buying a barrel of oil. I am buying the company that gets paid to pull it out of the ground.

Late in 2024, I published my view that the S&P 500 energy sector was cheap relative to the rest of the market.

I followed through with an energy stock as my December pick…

… and on March 16 I added a second position in the same sector.

But this one is different.

The company does not produce a single barrel of oil. It provides the tools, the crews, and the technology that allow producers to pull that barrel out of the ground.

So which company is quietly building the infrastructure behind the Middle East energy boom? Upgrade to paid to unlock the ticker and read the full deep dive.

TLDR

National Energy Services Reunited Corp. [] is the only pure-play oilfield services provider focused entirely on the Middle East and North Africa. That positioning matters because the region sits on the lowest-cost hydrocarbon production on earth, meaning activity continues even when oil prices fall.

The numbers already show the ramp.

  • 2025 revenue: $1.3B

  • Q4 revenue: $398.3M, up 34.9% sequentially

  • Operating cash flow: $264.2M

  • Free cash flow: $120.8M

  • Net debt: $185.3M (just 0.66x EBITDA)

The map above tells the story better than any earnings call. In 2018, NESR operated from a handful of entry-level footholds, generating roughly $450M in revenue with Saudi Arabia as its only true anchor.

By 2025, the footprint has transformed: multiple anchor countries now generate $75M or more per year each, underpinned by long-term contracts, and total revenue has grown to $1.3B. That is a 16% CAGR for NESR against a MENA market that grew at only 3-5% over the same period. The company did not just ride the regional tide. It took share, aggressively.

The next leg of that expansion has two clear engines. The company just secured the largest hydraulic fracturing contract in the history of the oilfield services industry, tied to Saudi Arabia’s Jafurah unconventional gas development. At the same time, it is expanding rapidly in Kuwait, where the national oil company has committed $8-10B per year in upstream spending through 2030.

Kuwait started as a blank space on NESR’s 2018 map. Management now expects it to become the company’s second-largest country by revenue, behind Saudi Arabia alone. These two engines, Saudi gas and Kuwait oil, could push revenue toward a $2B exit run rate by the end of 2026, which management has called the strongest growth year in the company’s history.

Despite this growth profile, the stock trades at roughly 6x 2026 EV/EBITDA, well below sector median of 7x.

My DCF model values the company at $41.50 per share, assuming:

  • 35% revenue growth in 2026

  • mid-20% EBITDA margins as scale improves

  • long-term growth stabilizing near 3%

The RankedStocks model reinforces the thesis with an RS score of 90, placing the firm in the top percentile of tracked equities.

The risks are real. The business is exposed to geopolitical tensions in the Middle East (the Iran war has impacted the region), the company previously had accounting control weaknesses, and pricing competition in regional tenders could pressure margins.

But if the Jafurah ramp and upcoming Kuwait tender awards play out as expected, the company could double in size within a few years.

Table of Contents:

  • RankedStocks Reality Check

  • The Business Model: How a Dollar Becomes Free Cash Flow

  • Fundamental Growth Drivers

  • The Competitive Moat: Why NESR is Difficult to Replace

  • Valuation & Sensitivity

  • The Steel-Manned Bear Case

  • Verdict & What to Watch

RankedStocks Reality Check

The quantitative screening strips away emotion.

NESR carries an overall RS Score of 90. This places the firm near the top tier of all tracked equities. The Growth score is 84, the Profitability score is 70, and the Sentiment score is a near-perfect 99. Outlook sits at 98. The Country Percentile is 99 and the Sector Percentile is 98.

The one red flag in the dashboard is the Valuation score of 28. The low valuation score is partially due to the recent re-rating. The valuation score relations on trailing and leading metrics. NESR shares have rallied more than 164% over the past twelve months.

The trailing multiples have expanded accordingly.

But the forward multiples tell a different story.

The Business Model: How a Dollar Becomes Free Cash Flow

Identity of a National Champion

Before we get into the business details, let me share a fun piece of trivia. The ticker NESR is not just an acronym for National Energy Services Reunited. In Arabic, نسر (pronounced "nesr") means eagle. Whether by design or happy coincidence, that is exactly what the company chose as its logo: a soaring eagle. I will let you decide if the branding team planned it that way.

NESR holds a unique position in the global oilfield services landscape. It is the first and only pure-play provider of oilfield services, with a total focus on the Middle East and North Africa. This is not a company trying to be all things to all people. It is the national champion of the most productive oil patch on the planet.

The business operates through two segments. Production Services, which accounts for roughly 70% of revenue, covers the work that happens after the well is ready to flow. This includes hydraulic fracturing, coiled tubing, stimulation, cementing, pumping, nitrogen services, filtration, completions, artificial lift, and pipeline and industrial services.

Drilling and Evaluation Services, making up the remaining 30%, covers the hardware and technology needed to put the well in the ground, including directional drilling, fishing and downhole tools, drilling fluids, wireline logging, slickline, well testing, rig services, and tubular running services.

This diversification matters. It is not a one-product company. It offers more than 20 service lines. This breadth gives NESR the ability to cross-sell into anchor countries and pull through new service lines from countries where it has established leadership. The company demonstrated this by building from near-zero in Kuwait to making it the third largest country in its portfolio within just a few years. Management has stated clearly that Kuwait should become its second-largest country behind Saudi Arabia, driven by the ongoing super cycle of contract tenders and rig additions.

The Revenue Engine: MENA Concentration

The 2025 revenue base proves the geographic focus. NESR earned $1.3 billion from the MENA region and a negligible amount from the rest of the world. This is a total bet on the Middle East.

But it is an informed bet.

The MENA region represents the lowest-cost hydrocarbon production on earth, with onshore Middle East breakeven costs of $27 per barrel.

Compare that to North American shale at $55 to $65 per barrel, deepwater at $50 to $60, or Canadian oil sands at a $40 per barrel threshold. When oil prices fall, MENA producers do not shut in wells. They produce through the cycle. And they need NESR to keep producing.

How a Dollar Moves Through the Business

Revenue comes from contractual service agreements with national oil companies. These are multi-year contracts, typically spanning 3 to 9 years, awarded through competitive tender processes. Once awarded, the revenue stream is largely predictable and decoupled from spot commodity prices.

The gross margin for FY25 was 12.4%, which reflects the competitive pricing inherent in long-term NOC contracts. A reader accustomed to U.S. completions companies, where gross margins can reach 25% to 30% on spot-priced work, might flinch at that number.

The comparison is misleading.

MENA service contracts are priced at thinner gross margins precisely because they are multi-year, volume-guaranteed agreements with sovereign counterparties. The trade-off is predictability over peak pricing. NESR compensates with utilization rates that remain elevated through cycles (MENA producers keep drilling at $27 breakevens) and a G&A structure at 3.6% of revenue, less than half the peer average.

The more relevant profitability metric is adjusted EBITDA margin, which was 21.3% for FY25. This margin reflects the true operating efficiency of the business once you strip out non-cash items and one-time charges.

The bridge from EBITDA to FCF is where NESR shines. FY25 operating cash flow was $264.2 million, up 15.2% y/y. FCF was $120.8 million after $143.5 million in capex. This represents a 43% FCF conversion rate from adjusted EBITDA. For a capital-intensive oilfield services company in rapid growth mode, this is an outstanding number. Management has guided to 35% to 40% FCF conversion from adjusted EBITDA in 2026, even as capex increases to approximately $165 million. The reason the conversion rate holds even as spending increases is that revenue is growing faster than Capex. The operating leverage in the model is clear.

The net debt-to-adjusted EBITDA ratio stood at 0.66x as of December 31, 2025, well below the 1.0x target management has set for itself. Gross debt was $310.1 million and net debt was $185.3 million, down nearly $90 million y/y. This is a company that is growing fast and deleveraging simultaneously. It is using its cash flow to build the firm, not to service crippling debt loads.

On a trailing twelve-month basis, ROCE was 10.2% as of Q4 2025. While this is not yet in the upper quartile of global peers, it is directionally improving and is concurrent with a heavy growth investment cycle.

As the Jafurah contract ramps to steady state and new contracts in Kuwait, North Africa, and across the GCC begin contributing, I expect ROCE to inflect materially higher through 2026 and 2027.

Fundamental Growth Drivers

The Jafurah Catalyst: From Zero to the Largest Frac Company in MENA

The single most important growth driver for NESR is the Jafurah unconventional gas development in Saudi Arabia. In 2019, NESR had zero business in hydraulic fracturing. It identified the opportunity, partnered with U.S. technology providers, and imported best-in-class Permian Basin practices to the Kingdom.

By 2025, it had won 100% of the committed scope on the largest single service contract in oilfield services sector history. This multi-year, multi-billion-dollar award makes NESR the largest frac company in MENA.

An important distinction: the committed scope is locked in, but the uncommitted scope remains competitive. The CEO clarified on the Q3 2025 call that all qualified service companies signed similar contracts for the uncommitted portion, and Aramco retains full discretion over when and to whom that incremental work is assigned. My model does not assume NESR captures uncommitted scope. If it does, the upside is not in my numbers.

The scale is staggering. Jafurah is central to Saudi Arabia's ambition to grow domestic gas production by 80% from the 2021 baseline by 2030 (an increase from the original 60% target, reflecting expanded scope across the Kingdom's gas development program). The field is expected to produce 2 billion cubic feet per day of sales gas with significant associated condensate and NGL volumes.

For NESR, this translates to a sustained, multi-year demand for fracturing stages, coiled tubing, well testing, wireline perforation, and flowback services. Operations began on November 1, 2025, and by Q4, the results were already visible in the revenue and margin numbers.

The “so what” for ROIC is direct. The Jafurah contract provides multi-year revenue visibility with a large, creditworthy counterparty (Saudi Aramco). The capital has already been deployed, meaning the incremental return on each additional dollar of Jafurah revenue will be higher than the initial investment phase suggests. Management expects to maintain the same profitability level as Q4 2025 as Jafurah ramps, with further efficiency gains on the horizon as they optimize pumping hours, rig-up times, and maintenance through AI-driven reliability tools.

Kuwait: The Second Engine

If Jafurah is the first engine, Kuwait is the second. The country has over 200 rigs operating today, making it the second-largest country in the Middle East by rig count. Kuwait Oil Company has committed $8 to $10 billion per year in upstream spending through 2030 to expand oil capacity by an additional 1 million barrels per day, targeting 4 million barrels per day by 2035. During the recent COGS Oil and Gas Show, the Prime Minister presided over several MOUs with international oil companies including Total, BP, and Shell.

NESR entered Kuwait from nothing just a few years ago. Today it has contract awards across multiple service lines, is tendering for several billion dollars more, and is building an innovation center (Ahmadi Innovation Valley) in collaboration with KOC. Management has stated it expects Kuwait to become its second largest country within the near term. All tender awards will be announced during 2026, with contracts spanning 5 to 7 years. This provides backlog visibility into 2031 and 2032.

The Broader MENA Growth Runway

Beyond Jafurah and Kuwait, every single anchor country in NESR’s portfolio is either growing or stable at all-time high activity levels.

In Abu Dhabi, ADNOC approved a $150 billion oil and gas investment plan for 2026-2030. Activity continues to march above all-time highs. In Libya, the country signed blockbuster exploration agreements with ConocoPhillips, Total, Chevron, and Repsol, with $20 billion in investment over 25 years. Libya’s target is to increase production from 1.4 million barrels per day to 2 million by 2030. Algeria has attracted ExxonMobil and is negotiating with Chevron, adding to existing Total and Eni activity. The Ahnet Basin alone could be comparable in scale to Vaca Muerta in Argentina. Oman, Iraq, and Egypt remain stable with pockets of growth in specific service lines.

There is an option the market is not pricing. NESR's Environmental and Decarbonization Applications segment (NEDA) has been quietly advancing pilot programs in direct lithium extraction, produced water recycling, and emissions monitoring across the GCC.

The 2025 10-K confirms NESR completed a first-in-country DLE pilot with a key Middle East customer. On the Q4 2025 earnings call, the CEO confirmed that the first lithium displayed at the Future Minerals Forum in Riyadh was produced by NESR, and that multiple active pilots with Aramco and Maaden are underway.

The CEO targets a long-term revenue level of $500 million for this segment if the economics prove viable. Today, NEDA contributes immaterial revenue. It is a venture-stage option. But the produced water volumes in the Middle East are enormous (the region generates billions of barrels of produced water annually), and if DLE reaches commercial scale, the addressable market extends well beyond oilfield services. i am not modeling any NEDA revenue. It is pure optionality on top of an already compelling base case.

Management has articulated a path to doubling the company from its current size within a couple of years, targeting $2 billion to $3 billion in additional tenders submitted across the region. The results of these tenders will be known throughout 2026.

Margin and ROIC Trajectory

The ROIC story here is one of a company transitioning from investment mode to harvest mode. ROIC rises from 5.7% in 2024 to 11.1% in 2026 and reaches 14.0% by 2031, driven by NOPAT margin expansion from 5.7% to 8.1% over the same period and a simultaneous improvement in asset turn efficiency from 1.0x to 1.4x as Jafurah-related and Kuwait contract revenue scales on already-deployed capital.

Before comparing NESR to peers, the methodology needs to be addressed, because three different ROCE figures are floating in the analysis, and each tells a slightly different story.

Management reported TTM ROCE of 10.2% as of December 31, 2025. My model shows ROCE of 13.9% for 2025. The YCharts peer chart, by contrast, places NESR at 7.78% on a trailing basis. The divergence comes entirely from how capital employed is defined and when it is measured.

Management calculates ROCE on a trailing twelve-month basis using average capital employed across the period. My model uses ending capital from the prior year as the denominator. I think my approach is more accurate as it measures what management actually had to work with at the start of the period, not a smoothed average that partially credits capital that only arrived in Q3 or Q4.

The YCharts figure of 7.78% sits below both my estimate and management's own reported number, and I cannot verify the exact formula YCharts applies to arrive at it. What I can say is that YCharts uses a consistent methodology across all companies and across all years in the chart. That consistency is actually what makes it useful here, not as an absolute measure of NESR's returns, but as a relative one. On that apples-to-apples basis, the chart shows NESR's ROCE rising steadily from deeply negative territory in 2020, and it shows a clear gap to close against SLB at 13.35%, Halliburton at 15.92%, and Weatherford at 21.35%.

The directional read is identical across all three methodologies: returns are rising. My forward ROCE estimates reflect the key inflection in capital efficiency. The Sales to Capital ratio in my model moves from 1.0x in 2024 to 1.4x by 2026 and converges to 1.5x and holds there through 2031.

That step-change is the mechanical expression of what happens when large, lumpy contract awards stop requiring net new capital and start converting to revenue: the denominator stalls while the numerator accelerates.

The four structural drivers of that improvement are traceable and specific. First, working capital efficiency has greatly improved, with DSO declining 22 days over the last 5 years…

… and inventory levels have halved since 2018.

Capital freed from receivables and inventory is capital no longer sitting in the denominator, earning zero.

Second, FY25 FCF was $120.8 million, representing 43% conversion from adjusted EBITDA, demonstrating that the earnings base is translating to real cash rather than being absorbed by working capital growth.

Third, management guided toward a $2 billion revenue exit run rate for 2026, with the CFO confirming the implied $100 million in incremental EBITDA is approximately correct. Incremental EBITDA on infrastructure that is already capitalized is by definition high-ROIC business.

Fourth, the ROYA directional drilling platform, which contributed to higher Drilling and Evaluation Services revenue in 2025, enters its commercialization phase in a $2 billion addressable market where NESR currently holds almost no share. Management has been explicit that this revenue line is not embedded in the $2 billion run rate target. It is additive, and it arrives on a near-zero incremental capital base given the platform is already built and tested.

The Competitive Moat: Why NESR is Difficult to Replace

First, switching costs.

NOC contracts in the Middle East are awarded through rigorous, multi-stage tender processes that evaluate technical capability, local content (in-country value), pricing, safety record, nationalization, and infrastructure.

Once awarded, contracts last 3 to 9 years. Switching mid-contract is not just expensive, it is structurally impractical. NESR has invested in local bases, research centers, employee nationalization programs, and manufacturing facilities that are embedded in the DNA of its host countries.

Second, cost leadership.

NESR operates with a decentralized model and lean overhead structure. G&A as a percentage of revenue was 3.6% in 2025.

This is lower than the regional and product-specific peers who must manage operations across dozens of legal systems and tax codes. NESR focuses its 7,000-plus employees on one region. This concentration translates into lower cost per unit of service delivery.

Third, local knowledge and regulatory access.

The Middle East is not a market that a foreign firm can waltz into. As the CEO has stated repeatedly, “For someone in the U.S. that does not know the Middle East, it’s an impossible task.”

New entrants face years of qualification, regulatory approval, legal entity formation, visa processing, and relationship building. NESR has spent seven years building this infrastructure across 16 countries.

For its established customers, NESR moves equipment between countries “in a matter of a couple of weeks.” For a Western competitor, it might take a year.

Fourth, the open technology platform.

Rather than developing all technology in-house, NESR identifies best-in-class technologies from around the world, particularly from U.S. shale operations, and brings them to MENA under its umbrella.

Partners like Cactus (wellheads), Phoenix (motors), and Scout (monobore) contribute technology while NESR provides the contract, infrastructure, and local workforce. This model gives NESR access to cutting-edge tools without the R&D burden, while the technology partners gain access to a market they could not enter alone.

These four pillars compound over time. Each new contract win deepens the moat. Each year of operational data in a given formation improves the knowledge advantage. Each innovation center (NORI in Saudi Arabia, AIV in Kuwait) raises the barrier for competitors.

The Shareholder Register: Who Owns the Eagle

Olayan Saudi Holding Company, one of the most prominent conglomerates in the Kingdom, remains the largest shareholder at 16.88% with an essentially unchanged position (a negligible trim of 258 shares).

SCF Partners, the Houston-based energy PE firm that helped bring NESR public, holds 7.92% and has not sold a share. Al Nowais Investments, linked to an independent director, holds 5.31% and is likewise unchanged. These three anchors, representing over 30% of the float, have held through the NASDAQ delisting, the accounting remediation, and the full re-listing cycle.

The selling is coming from a different tier. Encompass Capital reduced its stake by 22.84%, and Mubbadrah Investment trimmed by 16.86%. Fidelity pared its position by a modest 1.06%. After a 164% rally in twelve months, some profit-taking from funds with different liquidity mandates is expected.

What matters more is who is buying into that selling.

BlackRock added 2.55% to its position. Citadel Advisors increased its stake by 12.78%. Boston Partners more than doubled its holdings, adding over 1.1 million shares. Fresh institutional capital is rotating in at prices well above where the early holders accumulated.

Management ownership is more modest than I would like. NESR Holdings Ltd, the CEO’s sponsor vehicle, holds 2.94% and has not changed its position. Combined with other officers and directors, total insider ownership sits near 10%. I would prefer to see the CEO adding in the open market.

Valuation & Sensitivity

My DCF valuation gets me a fair value of $41.50 per share.

View DCF Model

The main assumptions are below.

I model revenue growth at 35% for 2026 (driven by Jafurah ramp and new contract starts), 15% in 2027, and 13.8% in 2028. Growth then decelerates from 12.5% in 2029 to 3.0% in the terminal year. The 2026 figure is consistent with management’s guidance that this will be their “best growth year ever” with an exit run rate of $2 billion. The 2027-2031 period reflects the expansion of unconventional gas across the region and the rollout of the ROYA directional drilling platform. The long-term growth rate of 3.0% reflects the structural expansion of MENA energy capacity.

Gross margins are modeled at 14.0% for 2026, expanding gradually to 16.0% by 2031 as higher utilization, operating leverage, and efficiency gains in Saudi Arabia and Kuwait offset inflationary pressures on chemicals and parts. The long-term margin settles at 15.0%, reflecting a service mix shift toward higher-margin technologies like ROYA.

G&A as a percentage of revenue is held at 3.5% throughout the forecast period, reflecting more efficient overhead than peers. Interest rate starts at 7.5% (current SOFR-based spread) and declines to 7.0% in the terminal year as the company continues to improve its credit profile. The tax rate is modeled at 22.5% for 2026, rising to 23.0% for the remainder of the forecast. While NESR is incorporated in a zero-tax jurisdiction (BVI), its operating subsidiaries pay taxes across the MENA region ranging from 0% to 35%.

I assume capex intensity at 10.5% of revenue in 2026, declining from the front-loaded investment cycle of 2025, and settling at 10.0% through the remainder of the forecast. This is consistent with management's guidance that capex as a percentage of revenue will decline y/y in 2026 despite absolute capex rising to approximately $165 million, a natural consequence of revenue scaling faster than the capital required to support it.

The 10% long-run assumption is deliberately conservative. Management has a credible path to bringing that ratio down to 8% to 9% as the contract base matures and maintenance capital replaces growth capital as the primary spending driver. If that plays out, the FCF generation in the back half of the forecast is materially higher than my base case implies.

Working capital assumptions are conservative. Days in receivables are held at 98 (the historical 5-year average is 82, but recent years have been higher). Days in inventory are held at 30 (down from 42 historically, reflecting the efficiency improvements management has delivered). Days in payables are held at 132 (reflecting the strong payment terms NESR negotiates with suppliers).

No dividends are modelled in the forecast period. Management has stated it will evaluate a formal capital return framework in mid-2026.

Sensitivity Analysis

Rather than running isolated sensitivity tables, I stress-tested the model through a Monte Carlo simulation of 1,000 iterations, randomizing three variables:

  • revenue CAGR (mean 13.3%, standard deviation 5%)

  • gross margin (mean 14%, standard deviation 2%)

  • WACC (mean 8.6%, standard deviation 1%).

The output distribution is shown below.

The simulation produced a mean target price of $48.62, broadly consistent with my base case DCF.

More instructive than the mean, however, is the shape of the distribution. Only 16.3% of the 1,000 simulated outcomes price NESR below where the stock trades today. In plain terms: under a wide range of randomized assumptions, including scenarios where revenue growth disappoints, margins compress, and the cost of capital rises simultaneously, the market’s current price is wrong more than four times out of five.

The flip side deserves equal honesty. My base case target price of approximately $41.50 captures 55.6% of the simulated outcomes, meaning that roughly 44% of scenarios produce a price above my target. The distribution has a long right tail, visible in the histogram, driven by scenarios where Jafurah ramps faster than assumed, Kuwait contracts add incremental margin ahead of schedule, or ROYA directional drilling begins contributing revenue earlier than the model credits. I am not counting on any of those outcomes. They are optionality.

The simulation also confirms which variable does the most damage when it moves against the thesis. A WACC shock is the sharpest mover. A 100-basis-point increase in the discount rate, well within the standard deviation tested, compresses the target price more than an equivalent deterioration in revenue growth, because so much of NESR’s value sits in years three through seven of the forecast when the contract backlog is fully operational. This is the legitimate risk scenario, and I address it directly in the bear case section below. Even so, the probability-weighted evidence from 1,000 simulations points to the same conclusion: at today’s price, the market is pricing in an outcome that the model assigns a 16% probability.

The Steel-Manned Bear Case

Bear Argument #1: Geopolitical Risk Will Destroy Shareholder Value

The strongest bear case is that investing in a region experiencing active military conflict is reckless. That argument has gone from theoretical to operational. On February 28, 2026, the United States and Israel launched airstrikes on Iran under an Operation Epic Fury, targeting leadership, security forces, missile infrastructure, and nuclear-related sites.

Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei was killed in the initial strikes. Tehran retaliated immediately. The ongoing strikes and Iran’s retaliatory campaign across the Gulf have produced one of the most severe disruptions to global energy markets in decades.

The damage to the supply chain is happening right now, and it is severe. By shutting down the Strait of Hormuz, the war has effectively erased the 20 million barrels of petroleum that used to traverse the waterway each day.

The export infrastructure of the entire Gulf is locked up. QatarEnergy, the world’s largest LNG producer, Kuwait Petroleum Corporation, and Bahrain state oil company Bapco have shut production and declared force majeure, while Saudi Aramco and ADNOC have shut down their refineries.

The collective oil production of Kuwait, Iraq, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates dropped by 6.7 million barrels per day by March 10, and by at least 10 million barrels per day by March 12 (source). This is the largest supply disruption in the history of the global oil market.

The downstream consequences for supply chains are not limited to crude oil. The Strait also transits around 45% of global sulfur exports, which is needed in the production of fertilizer and the refining of metals including copper, cobalt, and nickel.

Qatar, the second-largest producer of helium after the US and supplier of around a third of the world’s supply, halted production at its facilities in Ras Laffan following drone strikes. Middle East supply chain disruptions would likely tighten global helium supply and raise prices, potentially affecting major semiconductor industries in Taiwan (eg. our beloved ), South Korea and Japan.

I steel-man this bear case by sitting with those facts before rebutting them. A direct strike on NESR’s operational bases in Saudi Arabia or Kuwait would cause an immediate and severe decline in the stock price. No model can price that. The risk is present, the conflict is active as of today (March 19, 2026) and it cannot be hedged away on paper.

What is being done to mitigate the supply disruption

The NOCs and the international community are not sitting still. Three meaningful mitigation strategies are already deployed.

First, the bypass pipelines.

Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline network, or Petroline, a roughly 750-mile system connecting Abqaiq to the Red Sea port of Yanbu, and the UAE’s Abu Dhabi Crude Oil Pipeline (ADCOP), from the onshore Habshan field to the port of Fujairah, are being used to partially offset the near-closure of the Strait.

Saudi Aramco’s CEO confirmed the kingdom has ramped Petroline toward its full capacity. Yanbu exports have surged since the blockade began, and the ADNOC Fujairah route has climbed to 1.6 million barrels per day. The scale matters here. Petroline successfully insulates the kingdom’s exports from the immediate grasp of Iranian forces in the Gulf.

Critically for the NESR thesis, ADNOC confirmed explicitly that its onshore operations are continuing normally, and the pipeline to Fujairah is running to preserve export flow while offshore output is managed.

Second, strategic reserve releases.

The IEA mediated a coordinated petroleum release from strategic reserves across its 32 member countries. Around 400 million barrels of oil will flow into markets, approximately one third of readily available reserves and the largest release in history.

Third, and most relevant to the NESR thesis: the NOCs are not pausing their drilling and production programs.

They are protecting them. On March 16, 2026, three weeks into active conflict, NESR announced that it secured several multi-year cementing contract awards valued at $300 million, encompassing a significant award in Kuwait and several prominent awards in North Africa, described as “reflective of the positive activity trends across the region.” A company under existential pressure does not win $300 million in new contracts in the middle of a war.

Why the facts on the ground dismantle the headline fear

The critical distinction that the bear case obscures is the difference between export logistics and onshore production activity. The Hormuz disruption is a shipping crisis. NESR operates a services business. Its rigs, cementing crews, coiled tubing units, and stimulation equipment are already in the desert. They do not transit the Strait.

The production cuts we are seeing across the Gulf are being driven by storage constraints as tanker traffic has stalled not by any reduction in the underlying need to drill, stimulate, and complete wells. It is not because these oil and gas fields are under military threat.

The problem is the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz giving Gulf energy producers few export outlets for their barrels, forcing a chain reaction where domestic storage fills up and then forces the shuttering of production. When the strait re-opens, even partially, the NOCs need their wells ready and their production capacity intact.

The cascading economic fallout from the conflict is reshaping markets and supply chains, potentially for years to come. For the NOCs, this creates an intensified motivation to accelerate domestic production programs once export capacity returns. These governments cannot fund Vision 2030, their welfare programs, or their military commitments without hydrocarbon revenue. A temporary export blockade that causes production drawdowns will create a demand surge for oilfield services firms the moment the bottleneck clears. NESR is the embedded provider who will capture that surge.

The conflict also accelerates one of the structural advantages I identified for NESR at the outset: the impossibility of new market entry. Sustained shipping war premiums for transiting the Strait of Hormuz could affect the delivery of critical equipment, as LNG megaprojects operate on tight engineering schedules and depend on bottleneck-free supply chains. A competitor in Singapore or Houston cannot get a rig or a tool into the Gulf right now. NESR already has its assets in the ground. The conflict raises the cost of substitution for every contract NESR holds and eliminates the threat of new competition for the foreseeable future.

There is a real bear case here. I do not dismiss it. But the evidence points to a company whose local presence, NOC relationships, and onshore service model are structural advantages precisely because of the conflict, not despite it.

Bear Argument #2: NESR’s Accounting History Creates Trust Issues

NESR has a documented history of material weaknesses in internal controls over financial reporting. The company spent more than two years remediating its back office, was delisted from NASDAQ (and re-listed in October 2024), and faced an SEC inquiry related to its 2018-2020 financial statement restatements. Costs related to this remediation appeared as charges and credits in nearly every quarter through 2025.

This is a legitimate concern. A company with accounting issues should always carry a credibility discount. And in fact, I include a premium in the cost of equity for that.

I steel-man this by noting that investors have been burned before by companies whose reported numbers did not reflect economic reality, and a history of material weaknesses is a red flag that no amount of narrative should dismiss.

However, the remediation is complete. All four historical material weaknesses were remediated by the end of 2025, and this has been formally disclosed to the SEC. The remediation costs dropped to near-zero in Q1 2025 and are expected to be minimal going forward. The company completed a debt refinancing and cleaned up its capital structure by converting outstanding warrants into equity.

The CFO is an experienced finance professional (Stefan Angeli) who has overseen the transformation of the back office, and the company now runs on an updated ERP system with new processes, procedures, and controls. The worst is behind them. The question is whether the market will give them credit for the cleanup, and i believe the answer is: not yet, which creates opportunity.

Bear Argument #3: Margin Compression from Competitive Pricing

The CEO himself has acknowledged that large tenders in the current cycle are attracting “less disciplined” pricing. As the U.S. market softens and global OFS companies look for work, the MENA tender pipeline becomes a magnet for competitors willing to cut price to secure multi-year revenue. This could compress margins for NESR and the sector as a whole.

I steel-man this by noting that NESR’s adjusted EBITDA margins already declined from 23.8% in 2024 to 21.3% in 2025, a 250 basis point contraction driven by country and segment mix changes and competitive contract transitions. If this trend continues, the revenue growth story could be offset by declining profitability.

But here is where the evidence pushes back. Management has guided to stable margins in 2026 versus 2025, with sequential improvement through the year. The Q4 2025 adjusted EBITDA margin of 21.2% held despite the early-stage ramp of competitively priced Jafurah operations. As Jafurah reaches steady state and efficiency optimizations take hold (management sees potential for 20% efficiency gains in stages per day, rig-up times, and maintenance), margins should recover toward the 23% to 25% range that management has targeted for 2027-2028. The competitive pricing dynamic is real, but it is a cyclical headwind, not a structural impairment.

Bear Argument #4: FCF Conversion Weakness in Q1 2025

In Q1 2025, FCF was negative $9.6 million, with operating cash flow of only $20.5 million against $30 million in capex. DSO spiked because Ramadan closed most client offices in late March, delaying collections. Bears could argue this shows the fragility of the cash flow profile.

The rebuttal is straightforward. Q2 2025 FCF was a spectacular $68.7 million. The full-year FCF was $120.8 million with 43% conversion from adjusted EBITDA. The Q1 weakness was seasonal and Ramadan-driven, not structural. The company’s trailing twelve-month FCF trajectory has been strong for multiple consecutive years, with nearly $300 million in cumulative FCF generated over the past 10 quarters.

Bear Argument #5: Customer Concentration Creates Single-Point-of-Failure Risk

A rational bear would point to the 10-K and note that one customer alone generated 49% of the revenue, with the top four clients accounting for roughly 73% of the total.

In 2020, the concentration was even more extreme at 57% for the single largest customer. While geographic diversification into Kuwait, Libya, and Algeria has improved the mix, the reality remains: Saudi Aramco is not just NESR’s biggest customer. It is almost half the company.

The risk is not that Aramco will fire NESR. The contracts are long-term and the switching costs are real, as I have argued above. The risk is subtler. Aramco controls the pace. If the kingdom decides to slow Jafurah completions by three months to manage domestic gas storage, or if OPEC+ quota compliance requires a temporary activity pullback in oil, NESR has no offsetting revenue stream of comparable scale. The working capital cycle is also tied to this single counterparty.

The rebuttal rests on two facts. First, the concentration is declining. In 2020, the top two customers were 69% of revenue. By 2025, the top four are 73%, meaning the revenue base has broadened even if it remains concentrated. Kuwait tender awards in 2026 should push the Aramco share below 45% by year-end. Second, the counterparty risk itself is minimal. Saudi Aramco is one of the most profitable corporations on earth with more than $100 billion in annual net income.

The risk is not that they cannot pay. It is that they set the rhythm. For a long-term holder, that rhythm has been consistently upward across every multi-year planning cycle the Kingdom has published.

Verdict & What to Watch

My verdict is a clear BUY. The DCF target of $41.50 implies substantial upside from the current price, and the Monte Carlo simulation assigns only a 16% probability to the market being right at today’s levels.

The balance sheet is a shield: net debt of $185.3 million at 0.66x EBITDA, $264.2 million in operating cash flow, and a ROCE trajectory that is inflecting upward as front-loaded capital starts converting to revenue. Jafurah is running. Kuwait is ramping.

What to Watch

Tender award announcements across Kuwait, Saudi Arabia, and North Africa will arrive throughout Q1 to Q3 2026. Each major win adds multi-year revenue visibility and de-risks the growth trajectory directly. Alongside that, the Jafurah ramp to full fleet deployment by Q2 is the single most important operational milestone of the year. The margin profile at steady state will tell us whether the unit economics match the promise of the contract.

Two additional catalysts carry asymmetric upside. Management has committed to announcing a formal capital return framework around mid-2026. With leverage below 0.7x and FCF growing, any buyback or dividend announcement would be a re-rating trigger. And ROYA directional drilling commercialization, currently in extensive testing with contracts in Saudi Arabia, Oman, and Kuwait, opens a $2 billion addressable market that is not in any current revenue estimate.

The tide of energy is shifting back to the Middle East. NESR is the best way to ride that tide. It is the pick and shovel of the MENA energy renaissance, and the market has not yet priced in what is coming.
truncated_body_text: My March stock pick sits at the core of a thesis I have been building since late last year: the energy sector is undervalued, and the best way to profit from this mispricing is not to bet on the commodity itself, but to own the picks and shovels.
